title: Primary Function
learningObjectives: Connect wing-box function to engine-load transfer.
student: What structural function does the wing box perform with respect to the engine load?
instructor: The wing box carries the engine/pylon load through the wing to the fuselage. It resists the resulting shear, bending, and torsion while providing the wing's primary structural load path.

title: External Load
learningObjectives: Identify the assigned external load and its application point.
student: Identify the engine load used in this simplified analysis and where its line of action is applied.
instructor: The only applied load is the engine/pylon weight We = meg, acting vertically downward through the assigned engine center of mass.

title: Support and Boundary Condition
learningObjectives: Identify the fixed-root idealization.
student: How should the wing-fuselage connection be idealized for a first-order cantilever model?
instructor: Idealize the wing root at the fuselage as fixed, providing force reactions and a reaction moment. The outboard wing is the cantilevered member.

title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace bending and torsion from one eccentric load.
student: Trace the engine weight from the engine/pylon into the wing box and to the fuselage. Identify where bending moment and torque arise.
instructor: The engine weight passes through the pylon into the wing box and then inboard to the fixed root. Its spanwise lever arm produces bending, while its chordwise offset from the wing-box shear/reference axis produces torque.

title: Critical Locations
learningObjectives: Explain why bending and torsion need not govern at the same section.
student: Which inboard sections should be examined, and why might the same section not maximize both stress responses?
instructor: Compare the root and the specified mid-inboard section at x = Le/2. Bending moment grows toward the root, but the tapered wing-box dimensions also grow; transmitted torque remains constant while the mean enclosed area changes.

title: Relevant Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Distinguish bending normal stress from torsional shear stress.
student: Identify the normal stress caused by bending and the shear stress caused by torsion. Why do both arise from one engine weight?
instructor: The spanwise lever arm produces bending normal stress, and the chordwise eccentricity produces closed-section torsional shear stress. Both resultants arise from the same eccentric force but act through different moment arms.

title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify all active mechanics inputs.
student: Identify the load and geometry parameters needed to calculate M, T, I, bending stress, mean enclosed area, and torsional shear stress.
instructor: The calculation uses me, constant g, Le, e, br, hr, be, he, and t. The section coordinate determines the interpolated width and height.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Create the tapered cantilever model before viewing the reference.
student: Draw the wing as a tapered cantilever. Show the fixed root, engine station, engine weight, spanwise distance Le, chordwise eccentricity e, wing-box dimensions, and wing-box reference/shear axis.
instructor: A complete model shows a tapered cantilever fixed at the fuselage; downward We at x = Le; eccentricity e from the reference/shear axis; and a rectangular closed section with b(x), h(x), and uniform wall thickness t.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: Bound the engine-weight-only model.
student: State the assumptions used to reduce the real wing-engine system to this Mechanics of Materials model.
instructor: Use a fixed-root tapered cantilever, concentrated engine mass, static weight only, linear taper, a single-cell thin-walled rectangular closed section with uniform equivalent thickness, and small-deformation linear elasticity. Neglect lift, fuel, wing self-weight, thrust, maneuver/gust and dynamic loads, fatigue, buckling, connector/local pylon stresses, multicell geometry, composite anisotropy, and FEA.

title: Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the linked bending and torsion calculations.
student: State the calculation sequence from engine weight through internal resultants, tapered geometry, section properties, stresses, section comparison, and engineering interpretation.
instructor: Calculate We; calculate M(x) and T; interpolate b(x) and h(x); calculate I and Am; calculate bending and torsional stresses at both sections; compare them; and state a conclusion limited to the static engine-weight contribution.

title: Engine Weight
learningObjectives: Convert mass to weight.
student: Using g = 9.81 m/s2, calculate We = meg.
instructor: We = ({{wing_me_kg}} kg)(9.81 m/s2) = {{wing_W_kN}} kN.

title: Root Internal Resultants
learningObjectives: Calculate root bending moment and torque.
student: Determine Mroot = WeLe and T = Wee.
instructor: Mroot = ({{wing_W_kN}} kN)({{wing_Le_m}} m) = {{wing_M_root_kNm}} kN·m. T = ({{wing_W_kN}} kN)({{wing_e_m}} m) = {{wing_T_kNm}} kN·m.

title: Tapered Geometry
learningObjectives: Evaluate linearly tapered dimensions.
student: Using the linear taper equations, determine b and h at x = Le/2.
instructor: At x = {{wing_x_mid_m}} m, linear interpolation gives b = {{wing_b_mid_m}} m and h = {{wing_h_mid_m}} m.

title: Section Properties
learningObjectives: Calculate hollow rectangular second moments.
student: At the root and x = Le/2, calculate I = [bh3 - (b-2t)(h-2t)3]/12. Convert t to metres.
instructor: Using t = {{wing_t_mm}} mm = {{wing_t_mm}}×10-3 m, Iroot = {{wing_I_root_m4}} m4 and Imid = {{wing_I_mid_m4}} m4.

title: Mid-Inboard Bending Moment
learningObjectives: Apply the internal moment function.
student: For a cut at x = Le/2, determine M(x) = We(Le-x).
instructor: M({{wing_x_mid_m}} m) = ({{wing_W_kN}} kN)({{wing_Le_m}} - {{wing_x_mid_m}} m) = {{wing_M_mid_kNm}} kN·m.

title: Bending Stress
learningObjectives: Calculate maximum bending normal stress at two sections.
student: Calculate the maximum bending normal stress at each analyzed section using σb = M(h/2)/I. Which section has the larger value?
instructor: At the outer fibers, σb,root = {{wing_sigma_root_MPa}} MPa and σb,mid = {{wing_sigma_mid_MPa}} MPa. {{wing_bending_comparison}}

title: Thin-Walled Closed-Section Torsion
learningObjectives: Use Hibbeler's closed-section torsion relation.
student: For each section calculate Am = (b-t)(h-t), shear flow q = T/(2Am), and τavg = T/(2tAm). Which section has the larger torsional shear stress?
instructor: Am,root = {{wing_Am_root_m2}} m2 and Am,mid = {{wing_Am_mid_m2}} m2. With T = {{wing_T_kNm}} kN·m, τroot = {{wing_tau_root_MPa}} MPa and τmid = {{wing_tau_mid_MPa}} MPa. {{wing_torsion_comparison}}

title: Combined Stress Interpretation
learningObjectives: Identify simultaneous stress components without adding a failure criterion.
student: At each analyzed section, identify the simultaneous stress components produced by the engine weight. Do not apply a failure criterion.
instructor: Each section carries longitudinal bending normal stress that varies through the section height and closed-section torsional shear stress in the wall. These are simultaneous components of the engine-weight-induced stress state; the assigned scope does not request an equivalent stress or failure criterion.

title: Taper Sensitivity
learningObjectives: Relate moment and enclosed area to stress trends.
student: Explain why moving inboard increases bending moment while larger wing-box dimensions can reduce stress. Also explain why decreasing enclosed area increases torsional shear stress when torque and wall thickness remain constant.
instructor: Moving inboard increases the force lever arm and therefore M, but the larger inboard section also increases I and section modulus. For torsion, T is constant throughout the analyzed inboard region, so τ = T/(2tAm) increases as the tapered mean enclosed area decreases.

title: Engineering Assessment
learningObjectives: State a bounded comparison and model limitations.
student: For this engine-weight-only case, identify which analyzed section has the larger bending stress and which has the larger torsional shear stress. State at least two reasons these values are not total operational aircraft-wing stresses.
instructor: {{wing_engineering_assessment}}
